I'm Ganga, and I think I understand now why last term was so hard.
All year I wanted one thing: to come first in the science olympiad, and to see Saurabh Sir's face when he announced it. He was the teacher everyone respected. When he said "well done" to someone, they glowed for a week.

My mother sat with me that night and asked, "Who are you when you're not winning?" I didn't have an answer. I'm still thinking about it.

Chess coach's note, district academy, 22 January.
Ayesha, fourteen, lost in the fourth round today. She sat at the board for five minutes after her opponent left, not moving. Then she asked me, "Am I still in the top ten?" before she asked anything about the game.
She has improved faster than anyone this year. She practises three hours a day. She keeps a list of her rating on her phone and checks it constantly.
Her father Yusuf told me she barely sleeps before tournaments and cries if she doesn't win.
Her drive is a gift. But I'm worried she has no room to lose.
What I did next: I sat with her and went over the game move by move, pointing to two brilliant ideas she'd had. I asked her father to plan one full rest day each week, and I'll talk with her about why we play.

For Chhath, Usha, twenty-one, came home from her Patna college to the village by the river. At dawn she stood with her mother and aunts in the cold water, holding the bamboo basket of thekua and fruit, waiting for the sun.

Class 4 teacher's note, Thursday lunch.
Gautam, nine, would not share his tiffin with Anirban, who had forgotten his. "He never shares with me," Gautam said. "Last week he didn't give me his chips."
I sat next to Gautam. I didn't tell him he was wrong; fair trades matter to children.
I asked, "How would Anirban feel if nobody shared with him today?"
Gautam looked at Anirban, sitting alone with his water bottle. "Hungry," he said. Then, after a while, "Sad."
"And how would you feel if you forgot yours?"
Gautam was quiet. Then he tore his paratha in half and slid it across the table.
What I did next: I thanked him, and later told Anirban's mother about the forgotten tiffin.

qa.a: They accepted his fairness concern, then asked how Anirban would feel, moving his focus from the trade to feelings.

qa.a: He probably felt relieved and cared for, no longer sitting alone with only water.

grounding: It shows a teacher helping a child see beyond a deal by asking how a classmate would feel, without shaming fair play.

Sunday night
Madhav came home upset. He'd refused to lend his cricket bat to the neighbour's boy because "he never gives me his ball". He was so sure he was right.
My first instinct was to lecture him about sharing. I bit it back. He's eight; fair trade is how he sees the world, and it isn't a bad instinct.
Instead I asked, "How do you think Ravi felt, watching everyone play without a bat?"
Madhav shrugged. "Bored."
"Anything else?"
He thought. "Left out. Like when Arjun's group didn't let me play."
"How did that feel?"
"Bad." He went quiet.
After dinner he took the bat downstairs. I didn't ask him to.
Writing this so I remember: ask about feelings, don't preach.
– Hemant

Binita, you want a phone and you've offered to do all the dishes for it. Let me tell you about me and my bicycle.
I was fourteen, in Allahabad. Every boy in my lane had a cycle. I made my father an offer: I'll fetch the milk every morning, polish your shoes, and water the plants for a year. In return: one black cycle.
He agreed. I kept my side. Every single day. I was proud of the deal.
But one morning my mother had fever, and I refused to fetch the vegetables. "That's not in the deal," I said.
My father looked at me for a long time. "In a family, we don't only do the deal," he said.
I'm Lalit, your Dada. It took me years to understand that. Do the dishes, beta. But not only for the phone.

Kashish, you asked for your podcast about my first job. I'm Leela, and I'll tell you honestly: I kept a ledger in my head.
Who helped me. Who I helped. Who could help me later. If a senior asked for help, I dropped everything. If a new joinee asked, I was "busy".
I thought I was smart. And I was fair, in a way. I always paid back favours. People knew I'd return exactly what they gave.
But when my father fell ill and I needed a week off, nobody offered to cover. They didn't owe me. I'd only helped the ones who could pay me back, and those people were busy too.
I sat in the washroom and cried.
Now I try to help because someone needs it. My ledger isn't gone, but it's smaller.

qa.q: Who did Leela drop everything for?
qa.a: Seniors who asked for help.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling in the washroom?
qa.a: Leela felt lonely and hurt, realising the ledger had left only thin relationships.

qa.q: What did Leela change, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Leela started helping when someone needed it, not only when it might pay off, which builds deeper relationships.

qa.q: How might the new joinees have seen Leela in those years?
qa.a: They probably saw Leela as busy and cold, someone who only helped people who could help back.

grounding: It shows an adult who helped colleagues only when it might pay off, keeping a ledger that left relationships thin.

January. Aadhya, twenty-five, helped her team lead finish a report late at night. She noted it mentally: one favour, owed. When Sangeeta, a junior, asked for help with a spreadsheet, Aadhya said, "Can't, swamped." Sangeeta couldn't do anything for her.

Aadhya walked home feeling strange. The one person she had never helped was the one who helped her.
